carryoverIn.title: Breaking Changes
carryoverIn.pitch: A plain grey brick-breaker ships as v0.1. Between waves the studio offers two release candidates written in marketing-speak, such as 'Improved ball responsiveness' or 'Ceiling deprecated to improve performance'. You decode the euphemism, pick one, and play the next wave under its real rules while a board of system lamps shows what just went offline. A codex records what each phrase actually meant, and by v1.0 your build is a loud, glorious, thoroughly broken thing you assembled yourself.
carryoverIn.whyNow: Timeless premise, since everyone has met a vague update note, with a jam-weekend nod: one jam page reportedly lists 'Systems Offline' as its theme (as of 2026-10-11, per itch.io, unconfirmed), and each patch here switches a game system off or on.

research.summary: Hook, honestly rated: the Patch Notes jam page on itch.io lists 'Systems Offline' for a 72-hour jam on 9-12 October 2026, but the page also says theme TBA and the host's own announcements found by search only show earlier editions, so the theme is shown as reported, not confirmed, and the game stands without it. What is verified shapes the design: the 2012 juice talk by Martin Jonasson and Petri Purho showed how layers of feedback transform the feel of a plain game (its demo is reported, without a clear attribution in the results, to be a simple Breakout clone), which gives the greybox-to-gold arc and the juice ladder; two separate support forums carry user complaints about stock release-note wording, which anchors the euphemism grammar in something people recognise; a Mini Jam page reportedly rates a mandatory limitation rather than the theme, which this idea turns into a per-wave limitation delivered as a patch note. All studio names, patches and quotes in the game are invented.

design.coreLoop: Wave loop: you read two patch notes, pick one with 1 or 2 (or a tap), watch the system-lamp board change as its true effect applies, then play a 30 to 40 second brick-breaker wave under every rule accumulated so far. Clearing the wave or losing a ball ends the loop with a 'known issues' reveal that tells you what the euphemism really meant and files it in the codex. Notes follow a learnable grammar (improved means faster with a catch, rebalanced means nerfed, deprecated means removed with compensation, reimagined means shuffled), so minute two is decoding and minute ten is routing synergies, such as a sticky paddle with gravity, around your build's weak spots. Ten waves end in a v1.0 launch card; three rollbacks end the run early. The daily seed makes the offers identical for everyone.
sophisticationHooks: A decodable grammar: eight verbs (improved, rebalanced, streamlined, reimagined, modernized, deprecated, added in beta, fixed) act on eight game systems (ball, paddle, ceiling, bricks, gravity, input, audio, juice), so a euphemism means the same kind of change everywhere. A codex fills in as you learn, which is what separates minute two from minute ten.

Generic modifier engine with synergy and clamps: about 40 valid verb-noun pairs stack, such as a sticky paddle with gravity or multiball with the ceiling deprecated, while a stall watchdog ships an in-fiction hotfix if no brick falls for 25 seconds.

The juice ladder: feedback layers (hit-stop, squash and stretch, trails, particles, shake, synthesized sound) arrive as patches, so the page shows game feel being built from silent grey boxes at v0.1 to a bright, noisy v1.0. Each layer has a reduced-motion twin and a shake toggle.

Hero moment: a board of system lamps clicks off or on when a patch lands, an installing-update wipe sweeps the playfield, and the same bricks that were flat grey rectangles burst into confetti by v1.0 while the changelog scrolls alongside.
design.scopeForOneDay: Build: fixed-step brick-breaker with sub-stepped collisions, a verb-by-noun patch engine (8 verbs, 8 systems, about 40 valid pairs) with flavor text, two-card picker, system-lamp board, codex, juice ladder with reduced-motion twins, muted-by-default WebAudio blips, ten waves with rollbacks and a v1.0 launch card, URL-hash seed and share string, keyboard and touch controls, about panel with sources. Cut first: unlockable skins, boss wave, extra brick types. Not built: leaderboards, any backend.
risks: Hook is single-sourced and inconsistent: the page shows 'Systems Offline' as reported on a jam page, as of 2026-10-11, per itch.io (unconfirmed); the game does not depend on it.
Brick-breakers are crowded: distinctness rides on the decodable verb grammar, the codex and the writing, so the spec should protect those before extra polish.
Soft-locks and balance: clamp every parameter, ship an in-fiction hotfix that reverts the last patch if no brick falls for 25 seconds, and let the QA monkey test random builds.
Humor stays generic: invented studio, patches and quotes; aim at the genre of vague release notes, never at a real company or product, and list the forum threads only as sources.
Motion and flashing: cap flashes below 3 per second, give every shake or flash a reduced-motion twin and a shake toggle, start audio muted.
Scope: a generic verb-by-noun engine avoids hand-coding dozens of patches; skins, boss waves and extra brick types are cut first.

ideas.title: Memo Teleprinter
ideas.pitch: Type or paste any office memo and a clattering fictional teleprinter turns it into a five-voice rhythm: each letter's 5-bit teleprinter code lights five tracks, and buzzwords from a bundled jargon bank trigger absurd stabs and fanfares. A Euclid dial re-spaces the notes as evenly as possible and the 'cc' list cascades the memo down through ever more bureaucratic echoes. Every memo has its own groove; export the link and send your boss a tune.
ideas.whyNow: Timeless office-satire with a mechanic that is genuinely musical: five-bit character codes naturally map to five parallel gates, and Euclidean spacing turns gibberish into something that grooves.

research.summary: Teleprinter codes of the telegraph era use five bits per character (32 codes), with two shift codes switching between letters and figures; ITA2 is the standardised form, often called Baudot or Baudot-Murray. That gives a ready-made mapping from text to five parallel on/off tracks. Euclidean rhythms E(k,n), described by Toussaint in 2005, spread k onsets over n pulses as evenly as possible and reproduce dozens of traditional timelines, for example E(3,8), known as the tresillo; the construction mirrors Euclid's greatest-common-divisor method and Bjorklund's algorithm. Combining the two lets typed text drive rhythm and then be re-spaced by a Euclid control. The origin story of Bjorklund's algorithm (neutron-accelerator timing) rests on one secondary result and is left out of the page or shown as reported, unconfirmed. The humour comes from invented, harmless office jargon and a mock-solemn teleprinter persona; no real company, person or brand is used.

facts.claim: Teleprinter codes of the Baudot family use five bits per character, giving 32 codes, with two shift codes switching between letters and figures so the same pattern means different characters in each shift.

ITA2 is also called Baudot-Murray; one source calls plain 'Baudot code' a misnomer for it. It was standardised in the 1930s and later superseded by 7-bit ASCII (first published 1963); published bit tables disagree on whether the first bit is most or least significant.
Euclidean rhythms E(k,n) place k onsets over n pulses as evenly as possible; Toussaint (2005) showed the construction matches Euclid's algorithm.
E(3,8), written x..x..x., is known as the tresillo in Cuba and the habanera rhythm in the USA.
The Euclidean construction yields a family covering over forty traditional world-music timelines (Demaine et al.).
Sources label E(5,8) differently (cinquillo in most, a West African bell pattern in one Rust library), so the page shows the notation only.
Reported by one secondary source only: Bjorklund devised his algorithm for neutron-accelerator timing; shown as 'as of 2026-10-12, per a University of Alberta thesis, unconfirmed' or omitted.

design.coreLoop: Write or paste a memo, press send, and watch the teleprinter print it character by character while five tracks fire from each letter's 5-bit code. Jargon words from a bundled bank trigger special stabs, and the Euclid dial and cc cascade reshape the same memo into new grooves. Trying different memos, subject lines and dial settings keeps revealing new rhythms and new jokes, and each result has a shareable link.
sophisticationHooks: Exact 5-bit letter and figure table with shift codes, so the figures-shift in a memo audibly changes the pattern
Euclidean re-spacing of each track from the memo's own letter counts, with seeded variation so the same memo always plays the same tune

ideas.title: Drift Harp
ideas.pitch: A harp of plucked strings that you strum by dragging a finger or cursor across them, each string a Karplus-Strong plucked string tuned in pure just intonation and shown on a live fifths-and-thirds lattice. Play a looping chord progression and hear and see the pitch creep up by a syntonic comma (about a fifth of a semitone) every lap, a trick called a comma pump. A tempering dial lets you squeeze the drift shut and hear exactly what equal temperament trades away.
ideas.whyNow: Timeless: a tuning-system explorer where the surprise is audible. The visitor discovers on their own that pure intervals do not close a loop, which most explainers only state in words.

research.summary: A comma pump is a repeating progression whose pure intervals almost, but not exactly, return to the start, so the pitch shifts by a small interval each lap. The standard case is the syntonic comma (81:80, about 21.5 cents) in the progression C G D A E C; both Wikipedia and the Xenharmonic Wiki describe it. A 5-limit just intonation lattice puts fifths (3/2) on one axis and major thirds (5/4) on the other, so a loop that does not close is the drift made visible. Karplus-Strong gives a cheap plucked string: a noise burst circulating in a delay line with an averaging filter, where loop length sets pitch and the filter sets decay. Browser Karplus-Strong demos exist (one was seen), which de-risks the sound engine, but none found combines it with a drifting lattice.

facts.claim: A comma pump is a progression that returns almost, but not exactly, to its starting pitch, shifting by a small interval each repetition; the classic syntonic example is C G D A E C, rising by 81:80 per lap in just intonation, and the pump closes exactly in 12-tone equal temperament (Wikipedia and Xenharmonic Wiki, as of 2026-10-12).
The syntonic comma is the ratio 81:80, about 21.5 cents, the gap between a Pythagorean ditone (81:64) and a just major third (5:4) (Xenharmonic Wiki and Wikipedia, as of 2026-10-12).

Karplus-Strong synthesis circulates a burst of noise through a delay line with an averaging low-pass filter; loop length sets pitch and the filter shapes decay, so high harmonics fade faster (Wikipedia, a Stanford explainer and the Csound manual, as of 2026-10-12).
A 5-limit pitch lattice puts just fifths (3/2) on one axis and just major thirds (5/4) on the other (Wikipedia Lattice article and Xenharmonic Wiki 5-limit entry, as of 2026-10-12).

design.coreLoop: Drag across strings to strum, assemble a short loop of chords on the lattice, and let it cycle. Each lap the drift meter shows the pure tuning rising by one syntonic comma while a ghost of the starting pitch stays put. Turn the tempering dial to close the loop and hear what is lost, or chase a lap that lands back home using adaptive retuning. Every chord choice changes how fast and which way the pitch wanders, so there is always another loop to try.
sophisticationHooks: Karplus-Strong voices with per-string damping, pick position and a stroke-speed-dependent excitation, polyphonic across a harp of 12 strings
Live 5-limit pitch lattice with ratio and cents readouts; the drift is the distance between where a loop starts and where it ends on the lattice
Tempering dial that continuously morphs pure ratios toward 12-tone equal temperament, with a seeded generative drone that makes beating audible
Shareable URL hash holding the chord loop, tempering amount and seed
design.scopeForOneDay: Shrunk and de-risked. Build: Karplus-Strong plucks rendered on demand into AudioBuffers in the main thread (no AudioWorklet, so no CSP issue) with a voice pool, 12 strings, canvas harp and lattice views, pointer/touch strum and keyboard play, loop editor with 6 slots, drift meter with a ghost of the starting pitch, tempering dial, a muted-state visual story (lattice path, cents readout), URL-hash share, about panel. Voice cost: each pluck buffer is generated in JavaScript; short buffers (about 2 seconds) and a voice cap keep it responsive, as the stress-test project warns of glitches when the browser cannot keep up (that project was not found again, so it is not cited as fact).

The pump claim is solid, but the audible effect depends on voice-leading that keeps every chord pure; the spec fixes four tested loops, including the C G D A E C case, and checks the lap drift numerically in a unit test.

ideas.title: Over Your Shoulder
ideas.pitch: An essay about attention opens with a doorbell; how long and how rhythmically the visitor presses it is the page's first guess at them. As they read, the page quietly measures dwell time per paragraph, scroll reversals, pointer stillness and tab-aways, then shows a hedged margin note ('you slowed down here, about 60 percent sure') and rewrites later paragraphs to mirror the reader: shorter for skimmers, echoing for re-readers, footnoted for lingerers. It ends with a generated reading portrait and a shareable hash, and the fun is performing as a different reader on purpose to collect all the portraits.
ideas.whyNow: Timeless. Form-breaking early-web spirit: the interface is the content, and the rule (the page adapts to how you read it, nothing leaves the device) is felt within ten seconds.

research.summary: Net art of the 1990s made the browser's own layers the subject: several independent results agree that JODI projects expose code and fake error messages as primary content. A CHI 2012 eye-tracking study (36 subjects, 32 search tasks, Huang, White and Buscher) questions that the cursor approximates gaze, so the page presents every inference as a hedged guess. Blink-reactive weird sites exist per one scout search, not re-found; the claim that no site reads reading itself rests on a few searches only and the page does not state it.

ideas.title: Tolls In Kind
ideas.pitch: A short, sincere essay about how web pages learned to charge for attention sits behind a run of toll gates, and none of them take money. Each gate asks for payment in kind (patience, dignity, spare seconds, a held-still cursor) behind a sign that lies in one specific, learnable way: a decline button worded as a guilt trip, a price list that quietly inverts, fine print that is the real exit. A spotted rule drops the toll and a misread raises the price. Each cleared gate unlocks the next paragraph and a codex card naming the trick, and the run ends with an itemised receipt and a daily seed to compare.
ideas.whyNow: Timeless satire of consent banners and paywalls, owed to the humor slot this week. The form-breaking twist is that the interface is the joke and the essay is the prize.

research.summary: Deceptive-design patterns are well catalogued: Brignull's list (confirmshaming, roach motel and others), the five-category academic grouping of nagging, obstruction, sneaking, interface interference and forced action, and the European Data Protection Board's six categories. That gives the gates a real, named rule set to parody. Games about hostile cookie banners already exist (a Berlin university arcade game and a hackathon for the most annoying banners), so this idea differs by making every gate a small hidden-rule puzzle with a different toll currency, gating an actual essay, and by naming the real trick afterwards in a codex.

ideas.title: Smudged Memos
ideas.pitch: A clerk at an invented Bureau of Misplaced Things receives sealed memos in cipher, each one an absurd grievance built from a hand-written grammar, with a spilled-tea mishap blotting some letters. The visitor works a bench of frequency charts, repeat finders, shift wheels and crib-dragging to crack it, without being told which cipher family it is. Then they can forge a memo of their own from the grammar, pick a cipher and a blot level, and send a link that opens as a postmarked envelope for whoever holds it.
ideas.whyNow: Timeless: a daily memo gives a reason to return and the forge-and-send path makes the page spread person to person; autumn paperwork humor needs no news hook.

ideas.pitch: Halloween is on the way, so the visitor shops for costumes by fusing two words. Choose two cards from a stock of monsters, foods, appliances and falling rocks, and a blend engine hunts for letter and syllable overlaps, ranks the fusions by how recognisable both parents stay, and stitches a drawn costume with a name tag. Collect a rack of the best fusions, send a friend a link to your look, and chase the three judges' scores.

research.summary: The word portmanteau for a blend comes from Lewis Carroll's 1871 Through the Looking-Glass, where Humpty Dumpty explains that two meanings are packed up into one word; Britannica (citing the OED), Grammarphobia and Yale Alumni Magazine agree. Linguistic work by Gries (2004) measures blends by how much of each source word survives and how recognisable the sources stay, and DiGirolamo (2012) describes phonological and orthographic constraints, which give the engine a real rule set: find overlaps, score how much of each parent survives, penalise unpronounceable clusters. Deri and Knight (2015) built a finite-state system that blends two given words and report 45 percent exact matches against known blends; they note blend generation also involves choosing compatible words. Costume-season context from a retailer trend release (syndicated across outlets, one source) is left off the page, or shown as reported, unconfirmed. The word stock and the drawn costumes are original; no real brands or characters appear.

Strongest on polishPotential (9): The dossier names the hero moment: a wet-ice sheen stripe trails the machine and dries to high gloss, plus a gleaming canvas lap-pattern postcard and an intermission chime, which is a gorgeous thum... winnerNotes.headline: Approve: no blocker (season-start and machine-history facts check out, brand risk is containable), but the spec must pin deterministic attainable scoring, a one-viewport phone layout and honest wording.
risks: major: Score integrity. The scope says 'coverage mask on an offscreen canvas', which invites scoring by reading canvas pixels and a per-frame integrator. The same route would then score differently by device pixel ratio, antialiasing and refresh rate, and a mid-run resize or rotation (the QA monkey does both) can corrupt state. Corners and the boards margin can also make 100 percent unreachable, so a perfect grade or a shared challenge link would be unfair. -> Score from a logical typed-array grid advanced on a fixed 60 Hz tick; the canvas only renders. Build a reachable mask for scars, and add a Node test that replays scripted routes over many seeds and asserts identical scores and an attainable par.

major: Phone and laptop layout. A 200 x 85 ft landscape rink is only about 150 to 165 px tall at 390 px wide, so the rink is tiny and the tank gauge, clock and buttons drift below the fold. The same 'output out of view of its controls' S2 shipped on 2026-10-10 and 2026-10-11 with revise skipped, and browser-check asserts nothing about it (premortem item 3). -> Draw the rink with its long axis vertical on portrait screens, keep gauge, clock and primary buttons in the same viewport at 1366x768, 390x844 and 360x640, confine touch-action:none to the canvas, and have the builder run a Playwright bounding-rect and wheel check before QA; QA attaches the numbers as the repro.

major: Steering feel and depth cannot be judged headlessly and decide whether the first minute delights or frustrates. A half-circle U-turn only joins lanes about 2R apart (R = turning radius), so the ratio of R to swath width W sets how many lanes each turn skips: too small and it is plain mowing with one dominant strategy, too large and nobody can line up the next lane. Holding a straight lane with a finger or mouse is also hard, and a compact day has no revise slack. -> Choose R against W on purpose (start near R = 1 to 1.5 W), show a predicted turn arc, add a hold-straight deadzone and a free overlap allowance, offer a no-clock practice mode, and tune clock, tank and grade bands with a scripted bot that must find at least two viable routes (skip-lane mow, spiral or racetrack) and survive jittered input.

minor: Pitch ahead of scope. The pitch promises that friends can race your ghost via the link, yet scopeForOneDay makes ghost replay a stretch item and the judges credited it under delight. The rest of the build list (generator with five mishaps, kinematics, grid scoring, tank, sheen, canvas postcard, text strip, hash, procedural audio, About, accessibility) is large for a compact tier-2 day on 2 agent slots. -> Decide now: cut the ghost, ship a challenge link (seed, grade, route length), and strip ghost wording from tagline, description and About unless it is built and deterministic. Publish an ordered cut-list (ghost, then extra mishaps, then canvas postcard, then chime) and protect scoring, tank, practice mode and the viewport contract.

minor: Wording that outruns the evidence. The dossier says the 'first resurfacing machine (Model A) dates to 1949', but search summaries also describe an abandoned 1947 prototype, and it builds 'three layered passes' on a machine that shaves, washes, vacuums and floods in one pass. The 29 September 2026 season opening itself is solid (nine separate results agree, including nhl.com and Yahoo Sports), but hockeyschedules.net also carries a results table that the search summary flagged as unconfirmed. -> Facts policy in the spec: write 'Model A (1949)', label the three zones a simplification of a one-pass machine, show the season line once in About as 'as of 2026-10-12, per nhl.com and Yahoo Sports' with no scores, banner or player names, drop hockeyschedules.net, and give no real-world numbers (intermission length, tank size, speed) without a dated source.

minor: Less new than the distinctness score implies. Searches on 2026-10-12 found a playable 2013 Google Doodle where you drive an ice resurfacer to clear scuffs, a commercial game (Zamboni Challenge, Microsoft Store and Xbox listings) whose goal is to clean the ice efficiently, hug the boards and avoid re-driving the same patches, and at least one itch.io browser game. Yesterday's page also showed 'Swath width' and 'Overlap waste' as headline readouts, so the gallery gets two cover-the-surface scorers in a row. -> Make no 'first' or 'never before' claim, credit earlier rink games in one dated About line, lean on what differs (daily seeded rink with realistic wear, turning radius, water budget, sheen, postcard), and score as a 'gleam' grade with clean laps instead of reusing swath, overlap-waste or true-area wording.

minor: Brand and copyright. The maker's name is a registered mark for ice resurfacing machines (per Wikipedia via search, 2026-10-12) and the cited sources carry it in their titles; the name, its blue-and-white livery, a Z mark or a traced silhouette in UI, title, alt text, file names or project.json would be an S1 under safety.md however small. Related traps: league or team names and logos, real people or incidents (for example the emergency-goalie driver story), and a three-note chime that happens to be G-E-C, the NBC chimes sound mark. -> Say 'ice resurfacer' or 'the machine'; invent the machine's name, look and livery; allow the maker's name only inside cited source titles; league name only in the dated source list and no team names in the UI; mishaps are invented gags labelled as such; synthesize a chime whose contour and rhythm are not G-E-C and use no arena or broadcast melodies.

minor: Hockey authenticity for an owner who loves hockey: a fan will spot a wrong rink at a glance (marking positions, corner radius, creases). Search results quoting Wikipedia on 2026-10-12 give 200 x 85 ft, 28 ft corners, goal lines 11 ft from the end boards, blue lines 64 ft from the goal line (so 75 ft from the end boards, 50 ft apart) and a 30 ft centre circle. -> Draw to those proportions with red centre line, creases, nets and every faceoff spot, or label the rink stylized; do not print dimensions as page facts unless dated and sourced; seed the wear around creases, faceoff spots and boards so it looks like a used rink.

minor: First frame and first minute. An untouched scarred rink makes a dull thumbnail, the hero moment (sheen that dries to gloss) appears only after play, and a new visitor must decode scars, tank and a turning-limited machine at once. -> Open on an attract-mode demo lap or a precomputed half-resurfaced rink that sets window.__sedThumbReady, add a ten-second coach line and a no-clock practice mode, and provide an #autoplay or seed hook so QA and the thumbnail reach the postcard state without a human.

minor: Share link and accessibility floor. A hand-edited hash (long path, huge numbers, markup) can hang or inject, and a continuous-steering game can miss the quality bar on keyboard play, reduced motion and contrast. -> Strict hash parser (charset whitelist, 512 character cap, clamped numbers, unknown keys ignored, textContent only, no free-text names), try/catch localStorage under a versioned key, keyboard-complete play with a focus ring and aria-live status, reduced-motion variants, and scars readable by shape and luminance as well as hue.
mustFixInSpec: Determinism. Run the simulation on a fixed 60 Hz integer tick in logical rink coordinates (the clock counts ticks and pauses while the tab is hidden); the canvas only renders. Score from a typed-array grid of about 0.5 ft cells and never with getImageData. The same seed and the same inputs must give the same score at any pixel ratio, refresh rate, resize or rotation; add a Node test that replays scripted routes and asserts equal scores.

Attainable objective. Compute a reachable mask (boards margin, corner radius against turning radius, machine footprint) and place scars only inside it; report percent of reachable scar cells; no mishap may make par unreachable. Test the next 365 daily seeds with the bot: its par route must reach at least 95 percent inside the clock and tank on every seed.

Controls and geometry. Fix turning radius R against swath W on purpose (a half-circle U-turn joins lanes about 2R apart; start near R = 1 to 1.5 W), say whether reverse exists (default no), draw a predicted turn arc, hold straight inside a deadzone of about 8 degrees and allow about 10 percent free overlap (starting values; tune with the bot). Pointer steers toward the pointer at the maximum turn rate; keys turn at the maximum rate.

Depth proof instead of vibes. Write a scripted bot with three planners (skip-lane mow, spiral, racetrack), run them on 100 seeds and set clock, tank and grade bands from the results. Accept the numbers only if at least two planners reach 90 percent or more in time, the best beats the simplest by a clear margin on time or overlap, and a bot with plus or minus 3 degrees of input jitter drops at most one grade band; otherwise change R against W or the tank before building more.

Honest machine model. One pass lays one swath with three zones along the machine (shave, wash, squeegee, in that order) and spends tank water; it is not three separate laps. The About panel says this simplifies a machine that shaves, washes, vacuums and floods in one pass (HowStuffWorks, Wikipedia; as of 2026-10-12). The refill door is labelled a game rule.

Viewport contract (premortem item 3). At 1366x768, 390x844 and 360x640 the rink, tank gauge, clock and primary buttons share one viewport with no page scroll during play; on portrait the rink is drawn rotated with its long axis vertical; touch-action:none only on the canvas; a wheel over the rink scrolls the page. The builder runs a Playwright script (bounding rects of canvas and each control, scrollY after a wheel) before QA and logs the numbers; QA attaches the same numbers as the repro.

Facts policy. Safe as dated facts (critic check on 2026-10-12, search-only because every WebFetch host failed with DNS errors): the 2026-27 NHL season opened Tuesday 29 September 2026 (nhl.com and Yahoo Sports plus several more results agree); the Model A of 1949 had four-wheel steering that was cut back to front-wheel after it jammed against the boards (Wikipedia Ice resurfacer and the maker's history PDF); the shave, wash, squeegee order (HowStuffWorks). Write 'Model A (1949)', never 'the first machine'. The season line appears once in About with no scores, banner or player names. Drop hockeyschedules.net, and show the dev.to and cipherssecurity craft posts only as labelled craft notes or not at all. Game-scale numbers are labelled game scale.

Brand and people hygiene. The maker's name, blue-and-white livery, Z mark or a traced silhouette never appears in copy, title, meta, alt text, slug, file names, project.json or UI (the name may appear only inside the titles of cited sources); invent the machine's name and look. No NHL or team names or logos in the UI, and no real people or incidents (for example the emergency-goalie driver story). Mishaps are invented gags and say so.

Rink drawing. Use 200 x 85 ft, 28 ft corners, goal lines 11 ft from the end boards, blue lines 75 ft from the end boards (64 ft from the goal line), 30 ft centre circle (seen in search results quoting Wikipedia on 2026-10-12), plus red centre line, creases, nets and every faceoff spot, or label the rink stylized. Do not print dimensions as page facts unless dated and sourced. Cluster the seeded wear around creases, faceoff spots and boards.

Prior art and vocabulary. No 'first', 'new' or 'never before' claim anywhere. One dated About line credits earlier rink-resurfacing games generically (a 2013 browser doodle, at least one commercial game; as of 2026-10-12, per search results) without copying their art or rules, and links only sources that meet the verified rule. Score as a 'gleam' grade with clean laps; do not reuse yesterday's swath, overlap-waste or true-area wording.

Pitch versus scope. Unless the ghost is built and deterministic, remove 'race your ghost' from tagline, description, About and share text and ship a challenge link (seed, grade, route length). Cut order if behind: ghost, extra mishaps (start with 2, grow to 5), canvas postcard (keep the text strip), chime. Never cut deterministic scoring, tank and refill, practice mode or the viewport contract.

Link and storage safety. Hash grammar with a charset whitelist and a 512 character cap, clamped numbers, unknown keys ignored; any error falls back to today's seed with a visible note. No free-text names; dynamic text only via textContent. localStorage in try/catch under a versioned key. The daily seed is the UTC date and the page says so, with a field to type another seed.

Audio, motion, accessibility. Audio starts muted with a visible toggle and the AudioContext is created on the first gesture; the chime is synthesized and avoids the G-E-C contour of the NBC chimes sound mark. Play is keyboard-complete (arrows or A and D, Space to pause, a refill key) with a focus ring on the canvas and an aria-live status for grade and tank. Reduced motion means static hats, no shake, instant sheen; no flashes above 3 per second; scars readable by shape and luminance, not hue alone.

First frame and performance. Open on a half-gleaming rink (an attract-mode demo lap that stops at the first input and is off for reduced motion, or a precomputed state) and set window.__sedThumbReady; expose an #autoplay or seed hook so QA and the thumbnail reach the postcard state without a human; the first 15 seconds must pay off with the sheen trail on first movement. Keep the sheen to a short list of recent wet segments, cap the pixel ratio at 2, and avoid per-frame full-canvas readbacks.
